problems.title: Attach industry names to compustat
problems.prompt:
`compustat.csv` has firm fundamentals keyed by `sic` (industry code). `sic_indnames.csv` maps each `sic` to an `industry` name.

Read both, merge them with a **left** join on `sic`, and print the number of distinct industries.
problems.solution:
import pandas as pd

data = pd.read_csv("compustat.csv", parse_dates=["datadate"])
sic_indnames = pd.read_csv("sic_indnames.csv")
data = pd.merge(data, sic_indnames, on="sic", how="left")

print(data["industry"].nunique())
problems.tests:
assert data["industry"].notna().all(), "every row should find its industry name"
assert data["industry"].nunique() > 5
problems.test_summary: Checks every row got an industry name and that several industries are present.

problems.title: Leverage in the Computers industry
problems.prompt:
A firm's **leverage** is its liabilities (`lt`) divided by its assets (`at`).

The Computers industry has `sic == 3571`. Build the leverage column for those firms and print the **median leverage**, rounded to three decimals.
hints: Creating a column is arithmetic on two Series: `computers['leverage'] = computers['lt'] / computers['at']`.
problems.solution:
import pandas as pd

data = pd.read_csv("compustat.csv", parse_dates=["datadate"])
computers = data[data.sic == 3571]
computers["leverage"] = computers["lt"] / computers["at"]

print(round(computers["leverage"].median(), 3))
problems.tests:
assert len(computers) > 0, "the Computers industry must have rows"
assert (computers["leverage"] > 0).all() and (computers["leverage"] < 1).all(), "leverage should sit between 0 and 1"
problems.test_summary: Checks the filtered frame is non-empty and leverage lies between 0 and 1.

problems.title: Which industry is the most leveraged?
problems.prompt:
Merge `compustat.csv` with `sic_indnames.csv` on `sic`, keep the rows whose `sic` is in `[6020, 4924, 3571, 1040, 5812, 3760, 5411]`, and add a `leverage` column (`lt / at`).

Group by `industry`, take the median leverage, and print the industry with the highest median.
hints: `.idxmax()` picks the largest, `.sort_values()` shows the order.
problems.solution:
import pandas as pd

data = pd.read_csv("compustat.csv", parse_dates=["datadate"])
sic_indnames = pd.read_csv("sic_indnames.csv")
data = pd.merge(data, sic_indnames, on="sic", how="left")

subset = data[data["sic"].isin([6020, 4924, 3571, 1040, 5812, 3760, 5411])].copy()
subset["leverage"] = subset["lt"] / subset["at"]
medians = subset.groupby("industry")["leverage"].median()

print(medians.idxmax())
problems.tests:
assert len(medians) == 7, f"seven industries are in the list, got {len(medians)}"
assert medians.idxmax() == "Banks", f"banks borrow the most, got {medians.idxmax()}"
problems.test_summary: Checks all seven industries are measured and Banks has the highest median leverage.

problems.title: Winsorize market capitalization
problems.prompt:
`analyticskit.py` is in the working directory and defines `winsorize(values, lower_percentile, upper_percentile)`, which **caps** the tails while keeping every observation.

Winsorize `mktcap` at the 5th and 95th percentiles into `mktcap_w` and print the maximum of the winsorized column, rounded to two decimals. Compare it with the raw maximum.
hints: `from analyticskit import winsorize` — the notebook uses `from analyticskit import *`.
The winsorized maximum equals the 95th percentile of the raw column.
problems.solution:
import pandas as pd
from analyticskit import winsorize

data = pd.read_csv("compustat.csv", parse_dates=["datadate"])
data["mktcap_w"] = winsorize(data["mktcap"], lower_percentile=0.05, upper_percentile=0.95)

print(round(data["mktcap_w"].max(), 2))
problems.tests:
assert len(data) == 10647, "winsorizing keeps every row"
assert data["mktcap_w"].max() < data["mktcap"].max(), "the tail must be capped"
assert round(float(data["mktcap_w"].max()), 2) == round(float(data["mktcap"].quantile(0.95)), 2)
problems.test_summary: Checks no row was dropped, the cap is the 95th percentile and the tail shrank.

problems.title: Truncate instead of winsorize
problems.prompt:
`truncate()` in `analyticskit.py` **drops** the observations outside two percentiles instead of capping them.

Truncate `mktcap` at the 5th and 95th percentiles into `mktcap_t` and print how many rows are left.
hints: `data['mktcap_t'] = truncate(data['mktcap'], lower_percentile=0.05, upper_percentile=0.95)` leaves NaN for the dropped rows.
problems.solution:
import pandas as pd
from analyticskit import truncate

data = pd.read_csv("compustat.csv", parse_dates=["datadate"])
data["mktcap_t"] = truncate(data["mktcap"], lower_percentile=0.05, upper_percentile=0.95)

print(data["mktcap_t"].notna().sum())
problems.tests:
assert data["mktcap_t"].notna().sum() < len(data), "truncating removes observations"
assert data["mktcap_t"].notna().sum() > len(data) * 0.8, "only the tails should go"
problems.test_summary: Checks truncation removes the tails but keeps the bulk of the sample.

problems.title: Describe the tails of market cap
problems.prompt:
Fill in the blanks so the cell prints the 99th percentile of `mktcap`, rounded to the nearest thousand.

Compare it with the maximum you get from `.max()` — this gap is why the notebook winsorizes.
problems.starter_code:
import pandas as pd

data = pd.read_csv("compustat.csv")
p99 = data["mktcap"].___(0.99)
print(round(p99 / 1000) * ___)

blanks.hint: The Series method that returns a percentile of the data.
To round to the nearest thousand, undo the division with the same number.

hints: `.quantile(0.99)` is the 99th percentile of the column.
problems.solution:
import pandas as pd

data = pd.read_csv("compustat.csv")
p99 = data["mktcap"].quantile(0.99)
print(round(p99 / 1000) * 1000)
